Tutorial: Week 13 — Complex Numbers, Exponentials, and Differential Equations ​

For: Teaching Assistants conducting tutorial sessions
Related Lectures: Lecture 17: Complex Numbers, Lecture 18: The Exponential Function
Duration: 50 minutes
Core standard: Use complex numbers as the language of rotation, and use the course spectral-decomposition method to compute matrix exponentials.

0. Session Goal ​

This tutorial has six standard exercises, one for each idea:

PartStandard exerciseMain lesson
Aconjugate formulacomplex fractions become real formulas
Bgeometric motion ruleangle condition becomes a complex differential equation
C3×3 matrix ODEcompute eAt by spectral decomposition
Dparameter diagonalizabilitydelete repeated powers and test the radical polynomial
Etrace and eigenvaluesdiagonalization preserves trace by similarity
Fmultiplicity and projection tracecharacteristic multiplicity equals eigenspace dimension in diagonalizable case

The common pipeline is:

complex number⟶rotation/scaling⟶exponential motion.

For matrix equations, the required course pipeline is:

det(tI−A)⟶eigenvalues⟶spectral projections⟶eAt=∑λeλtPλ.

Attention

Do not solve matrix differential equations by coordinate tricks first. The coordinate solution is only a check. The official method is spectral decomposition.

Part A: Conjugation Formula (10 min) ​

Problem 1. Real and imaginary parts of 1/z ​

Let

z=a+bi≠0.

Use conjugation to prove

Re(1z)=Re(z)|z|2,Im(1z)=−Im(z)|z|2.
Solution

First use

zz―=|z|2.

For the real part:

1z+1z―=z―zz―+zzz―=z+z―zz―=2Re(z)|z|2.

But

1z+1z―=2Re(1z),

so

Re(1z)=Re(z)|z|2.

For the imaginary part:

1z−1z―=z―−zzz―=−2iIm(z)|z|2.

But

1z−1z―=2iIm(1z),

so

Im(1z)=−Im(z)|z|2.

For z=a+bi, this says

1z=aa2+b2−iba2+b2.

Part B: Geometric Motion Rule (15 min) ​

Problem 2. Velocity is always 120∘ from position ​

A particle moves in the plane. Represent its position by a complex number z(t).

Assume:

  • the velocity is obtained by rotating the position vector counterclockwise by 120∘;
  • the speed is proportional to the distance from the origin, with proportionality constant c>0.

Find the motion z(t) in terms of z(0)=z0.

Solution 1: complex-number solution

Rotation by 120∘ is multiplication by

e2πi/3=cos⁡2π3+isin⁡2π3=−12+32i.

The rule says

z′(t)=ce2πi/3z(t).

Therefore

z(t)=ece2πi/3tz0.

Since

ce2πi/3=−c2+3c2i,

we get

z(t)=e−ct/2ei(3c/2)tz0.

So the particle spirals toward the origin while rotating counterclockwise with angular speed

3c2.

The decay rate is

c2.
Solution 2: real matrix differential equation

Write the position as

y(t)=(x(t)y(t)).

Counterclockwise rotation by 120∘ is the real matrix

R120=(cos⁡2π3−sin⁡2π3sin⁡2π3cos⁡2π3)=(−12−3232−12).

The motion rule becomes the matrix differential equation

y′(t)=cR120y(t).

Now decompose

cR120=−c2I+3c2J,J=(0−110).

Since I and J commute,

ecR120t=e−ct/2e(3c/2)Jt.

From the spectral calculation for the rotation generator J,

eθJ=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ).

Therefore

y(t)=e−ct/2(cos⁡(3c2t)−sin⁡(3c2t)sin⁡(3c2t)cos⁡(3c2t))y(0).

This is the same motion as the complex-number solution: inward scaling by e−ct/2 and counterclockwise rotation with angular speed 3c/2.

Remark

The phrase “velocity is 120∘ from position” is not only a picture. After identifying the plane with C, it directly becomes a differential equation.

Part C: Matrix Differential Equation by Spectral Decomposition (25 min) ​

Problem 3. A 3×3 system with complex eigenvalues ​

Let

A=(00210−1012).

Solve

y′(t)=Ay(t),y(0)=(100)

by the spectral-decomposition method.

Solution

First compute

tI−A=(t0−2−1t10−1t−2).

Then

det(tI−A)=t3−2t2+t−2.

Factor it over C:

det(tI−A)=(t−2)(t2+1)=(t−2)(t−i)(t+i).

The roots are distinct, so the Lagrange spectral-decomposition method applies.

Start with the easy real projection. Since 2 is the real root,

P2=(A−iI)(A+iI)(2−i)(2+i)=A2+I5.

For this matrix,

P2=(152545000152545).

Now avoid multiplying the complex projection formula directly. Let

Pi=C+iD,P−i=C−iD,

where C,D are real matrices. Because the original matrix is real, the projections for i and −i are conjugate.

Use the two value-table identities coming from g(x)=1 and g(x)=x:

Pi+P−i+P2=I,iPi−iP−i+2P2=A.

Substitute Pi=C+iD and P−i=C−iD. The first identity gives

2C+P2=I,C=12(I−P2).

The second identity gives

−2D+2P2=A,D=P2−12A.

Therefore

Pi=12(I−P2)+i(P2−12A),P−i=12(I−P2)−i(P2−12A).

This is the useful trick: compute the easy real projection P2, then recover the complex conjugate pair from the value-table identities.

Remark

The real meaning of the conjugate pair

The two complex projections Pi and P−i are not real separately, but their sum is real:

Pi+P−i=2C=I−P2.

So

I−P2

is a real projection onto a 2-dimensional invariant space. On this real plane, the matrix A has only the conjugate eigenvalues i and −i. Therefore the exponential action on this plane is rotation:

eAt(I−P2)=eitPi+e−itP−i.

After combining conjugates by Euler's formula, this becomes a real rotation motion on the 2-dimensional invariant space. The remaining projection P2 gives the one-dimensional growth direction with factor e2t.

For this matrix,

Pi=(25+15i−15+25i−25−15i−12i1212i−110+15i−15−110i110−15i),P−i=(25−15i−15−25i−25+15i12i12−12i−110−15i−15+110i110+15i).

Now use the value table for g(x)=etx:

xi−i2g(x)eite−ite2t

Therefore

eAt=eitPi+e−itP−i+e2tP2.

Since

y(0)=(100),

we only need the first column of each projection:

Piy(0)=(25+15i−12i−110+15i),P−iy(0)=(25−15i12i−110−15i),P2y(0)=(15015).

Thus

y(t)=eitPiy(0)+e−itP−iy(0)+e2tP2y(0).

Using Euler's formula to combine the conjugate terms gives

y(t)=(45cos⁡t−25sin⁡t+15e2tsin⁡t−15cos⁡t−25sin⁡t+15e2t).

Remark

This example is deliberately not a visible rotation block. The rotation appears only after computing det(tI−A), constructing spectral projections, and applying the value table for etx.

:::

Part D: Diagonalizability with a Parameter (10 min) ​

Problem 4. When is this matrix diagonalizable? ​

For a real parameter c, let

Ac=(1c0010002).

Determine for which values of c the matrix Ac is diagonalizable.

Solution

Compute

tI−Ac=(t−1−c00t−1000t−2).

Hence

det(tI−Ac)=(t−1)2(t−2).

The roots are 1 and 2, but the root 1 is repeated. Therefore we cannot conclude diagonalizability just from the factorization of det(tI−Ac).

Use the square-free polynomial obtained by deleting repeated powers:

r(t)=(t−1)(t−2).

The diagonalizability criterion says that Ac is diagonalizable exactly when

r(Ac)=(Ac−I)(Ac−2I)=0.

Now compute

Ac−I=(0c0000001),Ac−2I=(−1c00−10000).

Thus

(Ac−I)(Ac−2I)=(0−c0000000).

Therefore

r(Ac)=0⟺c=0.

So

Ac is diagonalizable exactly when c=0.

When c=0, the matrix is already diagonal. When c≠0, the repeated root 1 still carries leftover nilpotent information, detected by r(Ac)≠0.

Part E: Trace and Eigenvalues (10 min) ​

Problem 5. Sum of eigenvalues for diagonalizable matrices ​

Prove that if an n×n matrix A is diagonalizable with eigenvalues

λ1,…,λn

listed with multiplicity, then

tr(A)=λ1+⋯+λn.
Solution

Since A is diagonalizable, there is an invertible matrix S such that

A=SDS−1,

where

D=(λ10⋯00λ2⋯0⋮⋮⋱⋮00⋯λn).

Use the cyclic property of trace:

tr(XY)=tr(YX).

Then

tr(A)=tr(SDS−1)=tr(DS−1S)=tr(D).

But the trace of a diagonal matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries, so

tr(D)=λ1+⋯+λn.

Therefore

tr(A)=λ1+⋯+λn.

Remark

This statement is actually true even when A is not diagonalizable. In full generality, it follows from comparing the coefficient of tn−1 in det(tI−A). For this tutorial, the diagonalizable case is enough and follows immediately from similarity and trace.

:::

Part F: Multiplicity and Spectral Projection Trace (10 min) ​

Problem 6. Multiplicity in det(tI−A) and dimension of eigenspaces ​

Assume A is diagonalizable and has spectral decomposition

A=λ1P1+⋯+λkPk,

where λ1,…,λk are the distinct eigenvalues and Pj is the spectral projection onto the λj-eigenspace.

Prove that if

det(tI−A)=(t−λ1)m1⋯(t−λk)mk,

then

tr(Pj)=mj.

Equivalently, the multiplicity of λj in det(tI−A) equals the dimension of the λj-eigenspace.

Solution

Since A is diagonalizable, choose a basis in which

A=SDS−1,

where D is diagonal. In this basis, each eigenvalue λj appears exactly mj times on the diagonal:

D=(λ1⋱λ1λ2⋱).

The spectral projection Pj becomes the diagonal matrix that keeps the coordinates belonging to λj and kills all other coordinates. Therefore, in the diagonal basis,

Pj∼(01⋱10),

with exactly mj entries equal to 1.

Hence

tr(Pj)=mj.

Since Pj is a projection, we also have

tr(Pj)=rank(Pj)=dim⁡Im(Pj).

But Im(Pj) is the λj-eigenspace. Therefore

mj=tr(Pj)=dim⁡Eλj.

Remark

This statement is also true for non-diagonalizable matrices if the eigenspace is replaced by the generalized eigenspace. In that setting, the exponent mj in det(tI−A) is the dimension of the generalized λj-space, not necessarily the ordinary eigenspace.

TIP

The key message for students:

e(a+bi)t=eat(cos⁡bt+isin⁡bt)

means

growth/decay+rotation.

For matrices, the same idea is computed through spectral projections:

eAt=∑λeλtPλ.
